subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: Back to School from Holidays — Students write names of places visited during holidays, note something special about each, and compare similarities and differences with friends' destinations (p. 131)

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites three or four students to share a place they visited during their recent break — not just the name but one vivid detail: a smell, a taste, a surprising sight. The class listens and begins to notice that the details are very different from one another.

Students open Textbook p. 131 and, working individually, fill in the table: the places they visited, one special thing about each, then ask two or three friends the same questions and record those answers too.

Pairs share what they found. Teacher draws four broad columns on the board — flat farmland, sandy land, seashore, mountains — and invites students to place each friend's destination in the right column. The class notices that the same land feels very different depending on who lives there and how.

Brief whole-class discussion: What makes each type of place feel distinct? Teacher closes by naming the four landforms the class will explore through the eyes of four children — Gurpreet, Ritika, Chandni, and Nayan — without promising what comes next or when.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare features of different environments and articulate similarities and differences through discussion and written recording.
periods.section_context: Holiday experiences across beach (Odisha), desert (Rajasthan), agricultural plains (Punjab), and mountains (Sikkim); four landform types — plains, desert, coastal region, mountains.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you closed your eyes and stood in your friend's holiday place, what would feel different from home?' Encourage children to name sensory details, not just place names — this opens the door to genuine comparison rather than recitation.

periods.section_ref: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet — Students look at the picture and write observations about the land type, people's activities, animals seen, and clothing details (p. 132)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook picture of farming life in Amritsar plains (p. 132)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 132 and take a quiet, unhurried look at the picture of Gurpreet's region. Teacher asks them to look without speaking first — notice what they actually see, not what they expect to see.

Students write their observations in their notebooks, answering the four questions on p. 132: the kind of land, the activities people are engaged in, the animals present, and anything unique about the clothing. Each answer should be at least one full sentence drawn directly from what they see in the picture.

Teacher leads a whole-class sharing of observations. As students read out their answers, teacher builds a short class list on the board under four headings — Land, Work, Animals, Clothing — drawing connections between what the fertile soil makes possible and how people's lives look in the picture.

Teacher reads aloud the section's details about makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi, and the Golden Temple's langar sewa — the community kitchen where anyone can eat, regardless of who they are. Students reflect briefly: what does it tell us about Punjabi culture that a kitchen feeds thousands every day?

periods.implied_lo: Students can record systematic observations from a visual source and connect what they see to the way of life of the people shown.
periods.section_context: Fertile plains of Amritsar; farming activities; tractors and animals in fields; traditional Punjabi attire; makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi; Golden Temple langar sewa.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to notice the connection between the land in the picture and the work people do: 'Why do you think so many people in this picture are working with the soil?' The langar sewa is a rich moment to draw out what collective service means — ask whether students know of any similar tradition in their own community.

periods.activity_title: My Region's Food — Connecting Near to Far
periods.section_ref: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet — Students name the most popular food in their own region and list the main ingredients used in its preparation (p. 133)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a quick oral round: 'What is one food your family makes that you love?' Students call out names. Teacher notes three or four on the board and asks: 'Do you think you would find this dish easily in Gurpreet's home in Punjab? Why or why not?' This sets up the idea that food is rooted in place.

Students open Textbook p. 133 and complete the task individually — writing the name of the most popular food in their own region and listing the main ingredients. Teacher circulates and, where students are unsure, encourages them to think of the main grain, vegetables, or spices their family uses most.

Small groups of three share their foods and ingredients. Each group finds one ingredient that appears in more than one person's dish — a common thread — and one ingredient that appears only in one person's dish. Groups report back to the class, and teacher builds a quick board list of local foods alongside Gurpreet's Punjab foods.

Whole-class discussion: What connects the food a region eats to the land it sits on? Teacher guides students to notice that the flat, fertile plains of Punjab grow wheat and mustard — and those crops become the foods on the plate. Students close by writing one sentence in their notebook connecting their own region's food to something about its land or climate.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect features of a region's natural environment to the cultural practices — especially food — that develop there.
periods.section_context: Most popular food in students' own regions and their main ingredients; Punjab foods makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi; fertile plains growing wheat and mustard.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: This task will yield genuinely different answers across a class — accept and celebrate regional variety. Ask: 'If someone from Punjab visited your home, which of your family's foods might surprise them most?' This near-to-far comparison brings the chapter's core idea to life through the students themselves.

periods.section_ref: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika — Students look at a picture of desert life and write observations about the land type, the plants, the clothing, travel methods, and what they like most (p. 135)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook picture of desert village life in Rajasthan (p. 135)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 135 and examine the desert picture silently for a full, unhurried look. Teacher asks: 'What is the first thing your eyes go to? What surprises you?' Two or three students share aloud before writing begins.

Students write their observations in response to the five questions on p. 135: the kind of land, the types of plants and how they differ from local plants, anything unique about how people are dressed, how people might travel in deserts, and what they like most in the picture.

Teacher facilitates a class comparison: the board is divided into two columns — 'Plains (Punjab)' and 'Desert (Rajasthan)'. Students contribute observations from today's writing and from what they noted in the earlier plains picture. Differences in land, plants, animals, and clothing accumulate on the board.

Teacher reads the section details about cactus and khejri storing water, camels as the 'ship of the desert,' and the colourful ghaghras and bandhini dupattas of Rajasthan. Students note in their notebooks: one plant adaptation and one cultural feature that make sense because of the desert's dryness.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record structured observations about a landform's plants, animals, and people, and identify how living things adapt to their environment.
periods.section_context: Desert land type; cactus, khejri, babool plants and their water-storing adaptations; camel, lizard, wild cat, python, eagle; colourful ghaghras, bandhini dupattas, turbans; camel as desert transport.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt: 'Why do you think the plants here look so different from the ones around our school?' Encourage students to reason from what they can see — sparse water, sandy soil — before the section text confirms it. Rajasthani dress is famously vibrant in contrast to the pale landscape; ask why people might choose such colourful clothing.

periods.activity_title: Water, Sand, and Desert Ways — Discussion and Inquiry
periods.section_ref: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika — Students discuss why water is scarce in the desert (p. 138)

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the question from Textbook p. 138 to the whole class: 'Why do you think water is scarce in the desert?' Students think quietly for a moment, then pairs share their reasoning before any student speaks to the class. Teacher records the class's hypotheses on the board without confirming or correcting them yet.

Small groups of three examine the hypotheses on the board and try to sort them: which reasons are about the weather (clouds, rain), which are about the land (sand absorbs water, no rivers), and which are about what people do. Groups add one more idea of their own. Teacher circulates and asks probing questions without giving answers.

Teacher introduces the section's explanation of low rainfall and the traditional solution — tankas, underground water storage tanks built in desert homes — and the folk wisdom of building them. Students note in their notebooks: one natural cause of water scarcity and one traditional practice that addresses it. Teacher highlights that communities developed these solutions over generations.

Students discuss the folk music connection: the section describes khartal and sarangi as instruments of desert folk music, and students who completed the 'Ask your family' task on p. 137 share what folk songs and dances are known in their own region. Teacher notes these on the board, celebrating the variety without requiring every student to have the same answer.

periods.implied_lo: Students can reason from evidence to explain why a natural condition (water scarcity) arises and identify traditional practices communities have developed in response.
periods.section_context: Water scarcity in desert; low rainfall; tanka underground water storage; khartal, sarangi folk instruments; dal-bati-churma, ker sangri; folk songs and dances from students' own regions.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: The tanka is a beautiful example of communities solving a real problem with local materials and generations of knowledge — ask: 'What materials would you use to store water if you had no pipes or taps?' This connects the traditional knowledge of desert communities to a problem-solving mindset without labelling it. Expect a wide range of folk music responses; all are correct.

periods.activity_title: Coastal Life — Marine Creatures and Beach Observations
periods.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students identify coastal marine creatures by matching names to pictures (p. 142)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook picture of seashore life in Puri, Odisha (p. 139); Textbook creature identification images (p. 142)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 139 and examine the seashore picture. Teacher poses the four observation questions from the page: the activities people are doing, the kinds of trees near the sea and how they compare with desert and plains trees, what fun activities students would like to do on a beach, and what is special about coastal dress. Students note answers briefly in their notebooks.

Students turn to Textbook p. 142 and complete the creature identification activity — matching six names (sea turtle, crab, dolphin, corals, seaweed, starfish) to their pictures. Teacher circulates and encourages students to look at the shapes, colours, and the habitat clues in each picture before guessing.

Teacher reads aloud from the section about the shankh (conch shell) used in temples, the Rath Yatra chariot festival, Odissi dance, and Sambalpuri sarees. Students connect: the sea provides materials (shells, fish), and those materials shape the region's culture and livelihood. Students add two examples of this connection to their notebooks.

Brief whole-class sharing: Which creature from the identification activity surprised you most? Teacher extends to the broader ecology — coral reefs support many other creatures, just as fertile plains support many crops — drawing a parallel to what students already know.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify marine organisms from visual features and connect coastal natural resources to the cultural and livelihood practices of people who live near the sea.
periods.section_context: Seashore at Puri, Odisha; sea turtle, crab, dolphin, corals, seaweed, starfish identification; fishing as livelihood; shankh in religious use; Rath Yatra; Odissi dance; Sambalpuri sarees; coconut and other coastal trees.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you lived by the sea your whole life, what would you make or do with the things the sea gives you?' This opens the connection between natural environment and cultural practice naturally. For the creature matching, encourage students to reason from visual features rather than prior knowledge — the skill of observation matters here.

periods.activity_title: Coastal Craft — Creating with a Coastal Twist
periods.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students use one coastal item to create a fun decor object such as a photo frame, necklace, painted pebble, mini basket, or sand art jar (p. 141)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook example images of coastal decor (p. 141)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the task from Textbook p. 141: using one coastal-inspired item or idea to create a small decorative object. Teacher shows the options — a photo frame, a necklace, a painted pebble, a mini basket, or a sand art jar — and invites students to decide which they will make. Students who have no access to pebbles or natural materials may draw their object in detail instead. Each student picks their approach before work begins.

Students work on their coastal-inspired creation using the materials available in the classroom — pebbles, dried leaves, paper cutouts, crayon patterns, string. The instruction from Textbook p. 141 specifies adding a personal creative twist. Teacher circulates, asking each student: 'What part of coastal life inspired this piece?' Students are encouraged to label or annotate their creation with a short phrase.

Students place their finished or nearly-finished pieces on their desks and do a quick gallery walk around the room, looking at three other students' creations. They note one thing they notice about a peer's work — the idea behind it, the material used, or the coastal feature it captures.

Two or three students share what they created and why. Teacher closes by connecting creativity to context: the sand art and craft traditions of coastal Odisha are practised by communities who have access to the same materials — the sea, the sand, the shells — and have turned them into living art forms.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present their understanding of a region's natural and cultural environment through a creative, made artefact.
periods.section_context: Coastal decor creation using a coastal-inspired item; photo frame, necklace, painted pebble, mini basket, sand art jar options; sand art tradition of coastal Odisha; coastal natural materials.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Accept drawings as equivalent to physical objects — the creative thinking is what matters, not the material. Ask: 'How does your piece show something true about life near the sea?' This question helps students reflect on whether their creation connects to content, not just aesthetics. Display the pieces during the beach-clean discussion that follows in the chapter.

periods.section_ref: On the Seashore, with Chandni, In the Mountains, with Nayan
periods.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students discuss what are the adverse effects of a cyclone and how communities can better prepare for such situations (p. 143)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the two coastal discussion questions from Textbook p. 143 — the adverse effects of a cyclone, and how communities can better prepare. Students think for a moment, then pairs share their ideas. Teacher lists the effects on the board: high winds, flooding, destroyed homes and fishing boats, crop damage, injury. Students add to the list from their own knowledge.

Teacher introduces Odisha's award-winning cyclone disaster management practices from the section — early warning systems, community shelters, evacuation drills — and students compare this to the class's own suggested preparations. Students note in their notebooks: two effects of a cyclone and one preparation step communities can take.

Teacher pivots to the mountain hazard — landslides — using the discussion questions from the mountain section on p. 148: why landslides are common in mountains during the rainy season, what can be done to keep people safe, and what communities can do to help those who lose their homes. Students discuss in the same pairs and then share with the class, and teacher builds a parallel board column for mountains alongside the coast column.

Whole-class reflection: What do cyclone-hit coastal communities and landslide-affected mountain communities have in common in how they face challenges? Students offer ideas — community support, early warning, shelters, government help — and teacher draws out the idea that people who live with natural risks also develop resilience and collective care. Students write one sentence in their notebooks about what communities can do together.

periods.implied_lo: Students can discuss the effects of natural hazards specific to a landform and describe steps communities take to prepare for and respond to them.
periods.section_context: Cyclone adverse effects in coastal Odisha; Government of Odisha disaster management practices; community preparedness for cyclones; landslides in mountain rainy season; safety steps during landslides; community support for disaster-affected people.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has your family ever prepared for a weather event — heavy rain, a storm, very cold weather? What did you do?' This personal connection grounds the discussion in real experience before moving to the textbook's examples. Highlight that both coastal and mountain communities face serious natural risks and have developed local wisdom and government support to manage them.

periods.activity_title: Nayan's Mountain World — Observing and Discussing
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students look at the picture and write observations about the animals, people's dress compared to their own region, and the trees found in the mountains (p. 145)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook picture of mountain life in Gangtok, Sikkim (p. 145)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 145 and examine the mountain picture from Nayan's diary. Teacher asks them to notice the landscape first — rocky, steep, forested — before looking at the people and animals. Two students describe what the land looks like before the class moves to the written task.

Students write their observations for the three questions on p. 145: the types of animals in the picture, how the mountain dress (bakhu, dumdyam, Gunyo cholo) differs from what they wear in their own region, and a description of the trees visible. Students are encouraged to write in their own words and to make the comparison to their own experience genuine, not formulaic.

Teacher facilitates a class discussion using the p. 147 questions about how the cold climate affects how people live and dress, why certain trees like pine and oak grow better in the mountains, and how animals like yak survive in cold conditions. Teacher connects students' written observations to the explanations in the section — cold climate requires warm materials, slanting roofs shed snow and rain, yaks are built for altitude and cold.

Teacher introduces the Loosong and Namsoong festivals and the chaam mask dance, and thukpa and sel roti as mountain foods. Students reflect briefly: how are these foods and festivals connected to the cold mountain climate? Students write one connection in their notebooks — e.g., thukpa is a warm noodle soup suited to cold weather.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe how climate conditions in a mountain region shape the animals, plants, clothing, food, and shelter of the people who live there.
periods.section_context: Mountain picture from Gangtok, Sikkim; yak and mountain animals; bakhu, dumdyam, Gunyo cholo traditional dress; oak, pine, walnut, chestnut trees; thukpa, sel roti; Loosong and Namsoong festivals; chaam mask dance; wooden slanting-roof houses.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you had to live in Nayan's mountain village for a winter, what from your own home would you find most useful? What would you need to change?' This imaginative comparison helps students reason about climate adaptation without needing to memorise facts. Encourage students to notice that every element of mountain life — food, dress, house shape — is a response to the same cold, wet, steep environment.

periods.activity_title: My Landform, My Imagined Land — Drawing and Comparing
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students draw the landform around them, naming the area, type of landform, and interesting features of people, professions, food, houses, plants, and animals (p. 149)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the two tasks from Textbook p. 149 and p. 151: first, students will draw their own local landform with labels; second, they will design an imaginary landform by combining their favourite features from all four regions. Teacher asks: 'If you could combine one thing from each region — plains, desert, coast, mountains — what would you choose?' Students call out ideas briefly before drawing begins.

Students work on Textbook p. 149's task — drawing their local landform in their notebooks and labelling it with the area's name, the landform type, and at least four features from the list: people, professions, food, houses, plants, animals. Teacher circulates and encourages labelling in the student's own words rather than copying.

Students move to the imaginary landform task from Textbook p. 151 — designing and drawing a composite landform that combines favourite features from mountains, plains, coasts, and deserts. Each student's drawing should include at least one feature from two different regions and a short written note (two to three words per feature) explaining why they chose it.

Three or four students share their imaginary landforms with the class, answering the reflection questions from p. 151: what made them choose those features, how each feature benefits people or animals, and what difficulties their imaginary land might pose for its inhabitants. Teacher closes by naming what the class has done across this chapter — travelled through four very different Indian lands — without claiming any journey is complete.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent a real or imagined environment creatively through drawing and labelling, and reason about how geographical features shape life for the people, animals, and plants within them.
periods.section_context: Drawing of students' own local landform with labels for people, professions, food, houses, plants, animals; imaginary composite landform combining features from plains, desert, coastal, and mountain regions; reflection on why features were chosen and what benefits and difficulties they create.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Accept all landform types as valid for students' local drawings — some students may live on plains, others near hills or a river, others in a town. Ask: 'What one thing about your landform makes life here easier? What makes it harder?' The imaginary landform task is a creative-reasoning exercise — encourage students to be bold in their combinations while thinking through the consequences.

assessment_items.question_text: Gurpreet's class is sharing holiday memories. One child says: 'We visited a place with flat, wide fields, where tractors worked alongside animals in the soil, and people wore bright, flowing clothes while farming.' Which landform type does this description best match?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. The description — flat fields, tractors, farming, bright attire — matches the fertile plains of Punjab as presented in the chapter's holiday-sharing introduction.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare features of different environments and articulate similarities and differences through discussion and written recording.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'Desert' suggests the student is associating farming with dry land, possibly confusing the region with Rajasthan — an error of landform-culture matching.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'Mountain' suggests the student is associating farming activity with highlands, not connecting the flat, wide fields described to the plains landform.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'Coastal region' suggests the student may be linking colourful clothing to coastal culture rather than attending to the land description of flat fields and tractors.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at a picture of farming life in the Punjab plains. A student writes these observations: 'I see flat land, many people working, and a big golden building.' Write two more observations the student could add from a picture of this region — one about the animals and one about the clothing of the people.
expected_elements: An observation about animals present in the picture — such as bullocks, cows, or other farm animals seen working in the fields alongside tractors.
An observation about the clothing of the people — such as the traditional Punjabi attire, bright colours, or distinctive dress worn by men and women in the picture.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any accurate observation about animals seen in the farming picture (bullocks, cows) and any accurate description of clothing (Punjabi traditional dress, colourful garments). Both observations must be drawn from the picture content, not invented.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record systematic observations from a visual source and connect what they see to the way of life of the people shown.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

expected_elements: A named or described animal seen in the farming picture — bullocks, cows, or farm animals working alongside people or tractors.
A description of the clothing of people in the picture — Punjabi traditional attire, bright colours, or distinctive garments worn by the people shown.

assessment_items.question_text: Gurpreet tells her class that the most popular foods in Punjab — makki di roti and sarson da saag — come from crops grown on the fertile plains. Which statement best explains why these foods are popular in Punjab?

options.label: A
options.text: Punjabi people chose these foods because they look colourful and festive.

options.label: B
options.text: These foods are made from crops — maize and mustard — that grow well in Punjab's flat, fertile land.

options.label: C
options.text: These foods were borrowed from the desert regions of Rajasthan where people needed hearty meals.

options.label: D
options.text: These foods became popular because the Golden Temple serves them at its community kitchen.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The chapter establishes that the fertile plains of Punjab grow wheat, maize, and mustard — the very crops that make the region's signature foods possible. The connection between land and food is the central skill being tested.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect features of a region's natural environment to the cultural practices — especially food — that develop there.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option shows the student is thinking about food preference as a matter of taste or appearance, missing the environmental connection between land productivity and food culture.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option shows confusion between landform regions — associating Punjab's foods with Rajasthan indicates the student has not connected the correct region's environment to its food.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option conflates the cultural institution of the langar with the origin of the food itself — the student understands one fact (langar serves food) but misapplies it to explain why certain foods exist.

assessment_items.question_text: Ritika's class is looking at a picture of life in the Rajasthan desert. A student notices that the plants in the picture look very different from the plants near their school. Write two differences a student might observe between desert plants (like cactus or khejri) and the plants in their own area.
expected_elements: A difference related to water or moisture — desert plants have thick stems, waxy surfaces, or special structures to store water, unlike plants in wetter regions that have broad, flat leaves.
A difference related to appearance or size — desert plants are often spiny, low-growing, or thorny, unlike leafy or tall trees and shrubs found in better-watered areas.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two genuine observations that contrast desert plants with plants in wetter or more moderate environments. Answers should reflect what can be seen in or reasoned from the picture content. Regional variation in what 'local plants' look like is expected — mark on the quality of the contrast drawn, not on the specific local plant named.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record structured observations about a landform's plants, animals, and people, and identify how living things adapt to their environment.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

expected_elements: A contrast in water-related adaptation — desert plants store water (thick stems, waxy surface, deep roots) while plants in wetter regions have broader leaves and do not need to store water.
A contrast in physical appearance — desert plants are spiny, thorny, or low-growing, unlike the leafy or tall trees and plants common in wetter local environments.

assessment_items.question_text: Desert communities in Rajasthan face very little rainfall throughout the year. Explain why water is scarce in the desert, and describe one traditional practice that communities there have developed to manage this scarcity. What does this tell you about the people who live in the desert?
look_for: A clear explanation of why water is scarce — low rainfall, high evaporation, sandy soil that does not retain water, absence of rivers — showing the student understands the natural cause, not just the fact.
A description of the tanka (underground water storage tank) or similar traditional water conservation practice, with some indication of how it works or why it is useful.

A reasoned statement about the desert community — that they are resourceful, adapted to their environment, have developed knowledge over generations, or demonstrate collective problem-solving — going beyond a simple factual recall.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response explains the cause of scarcity (not just states it), names a real traditional practice with some detail, and draws a considered inference about the community. A weak response states only that 'there is no water in the desert' and names the tanka without explanation.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can reason from evidence to explain why a natural condition (water scarcity) arises and identify traditional practices communities have developed in response.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

look_for: A causal explanation of water scarcity — the student identifies low rainfall and possibly high evaporation or sandy soil rather than simply stating water is not available.
A specific traditional practice — the tanka (underground storage tank) is the chapter's primary example; credit any accurate traditional water-management practice from the section.

An inference about the community's character or knowledge — phrases like 'people found a clever solution', 'they learned from experience', or 'communities worked together to survive' indicate the student is reasoning beyond recall.

assessment_items.question_text: Chandni visits a beach in Odisha and sees many creatures near the sea. She tries to identify them from their appearance. Which of these creatures is most likely to be seen attached to rocks or the ocean floor, forming colourful branching structures that many other sea creatures depend on?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is D. The description — attached to rocks, colourful branching structures, many creatures depend on them — matches corals as presented in the creature identification activity. The item tests identification from visual and descriptive features, not name recall alone.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify marine organisms from visual features and connect coastal natural resources to the cultural and livelihood practices of people who live near the sea.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'Sea turtle' suggests the student is associating the feature of being found on the ocean floor with a large, slow-moving creature, without attending to the 'attached to rocks' and 'branching' descriptors.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'Starfish' suggests the student connected 'attached to the ocean floor' with starfish, missing the 'branching structures' and 'many creatures depend on them' clues that distinguish corals.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'Dolphin' suggests the student is thinking of a well-known sea creature without reading the description carefully — dolphins are free-swimming and do not form attached branching structures.

assessment_items.task: Create a coastal-inspired object using materials available in your classroom — a decorated pebble, a paper frame with a sea creature drawn on it, a paper necklace with shell shapes, or any other object that captures something about life near the sea. Write or say two things about your creation: what part of coastal life inspired it, and how it connects to what people who live near the sea make or use.
assessment_items.scaffold: Choose one: a decorated pebble / a paper frame with a sea creature / a paper necklace with shell or ocean shapes / your own idea. Make your object. Then answer: (1) What part of coastal life gave you this idea? (2) How does your object connect to something people near the sea actually make or use?
format_of_output: A created or drawn coastal-inspired object
Two written or spoken sentences: one naming the coastal inspiration, one connecting the object to real coastal life or craft
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any object — physical or drawn — that reflects a genuine connection to coastal life as presented in the chapter (fishing, sand art, shells, sea creatures, Odisha's craft traditions). The written or spoken component is essential: it shows whether the student can articulate the connection between their creation and the chapter content. A drawing is fully acceptable as the created object.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present their understanding of a region's natural and cultural environment through a creative, made artefact.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can translate chapter knowledge about coastal life into a creative artefact and articulate the connection between that artefact and the natural or cultural environment of a coastal region.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold gives students a menu of options (decorated pebble, paper frame, necklace, free choice) and two specific questions to answer. The teacher should check that the student's verbal or written response addresses both questions — inspiration source and real-world connection — not just that an object was made.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: the object clearly reflects a coastal feature (a sea creature, a shell pattern, a sand-like texture), and the student can name a specific connection to coastal life or craft (e.g., 'Odisha's sand art uses sand and natural dyes'). Weak: the object is made but the student cannot explain the coastal connection, or the connection is generic ('because it looks like the sea').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students without access to pebbles or craft materials should draw their object in detail. Students who find written expression difficult may dictate their two sentences to the teacher or a peer. All output formats — physical, drawn, spoken — are equally valid.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Creative artefact (physical or drawn) with two written or spoken explanatory statements
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The creative mode matches the C&E dominant mode of the period and the C-6.2 competency's emphasis on presenting understanding through creative expression. The written or spoken component ensures the creation is grounded in chapter content rather than purely decorative.

assessment_items.question_text: Chandni's village in Odisha often faces cyclones, and Nayan's mountain region in Sikkim sometimes has landslides during the rainy season. Both are natural hazards tied to where people live. Choose ONE of these hazards. Explain what causes it, describe two harmful effects it can have, and suggest two things communities can do to prepare for or respond to it.
look_for: A clear identification of which hazard the student has chosen and a reasonable explanation of its cause — cyclones form over warm seas and bring strong winds and heavy rain; landslides occur when heavy rain loosens soil and rock on steep slopes.

Two distinct harmful effects described with some specificity — not just 'damage' but flooding, destroyed homes, loss of boats or crops (cyclone), or blocked roads, destroyed homes, injury to people (landslide).

Two preparedness or response steps that are genuinely actionable — early warning systems, evacuation drills, community shelters, helping neighbours, government rescue teams — showing the student understands that preparation reduces harm.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept either cyclone or landslide as the chosen hazard — do not penalise for choice. A strong response names a cause, gives two specific effects, and proposes two steps with reasoning. A weak response lists effects without cause and gives vague steps like 'be careful'. Both hazards are fully covered in the chapter.
assessment_items.chapter_section: On the Seashore, with Chandni, In the Mountains, with Nayan
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can discuss the effects of natural hazards specific to a landform and describe steps communities take to prepare for and respond to them.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

look_for: A named hazard (cyclone or landslide) with a causal explanation — not just that it happens but why (cyclones: warm seas, strong winds; landslides: steep slopes, heavy rain, loose soil).

Two harmful effects described with some specificity — flooding, loss of fishing boats, destroyed homes (cyclone); blocked roads, fallen rocks, destroyed houses (landslide) — rather than a single generic mention of 'damage'.
Two actionable community preparedness or response steps — evacuation drills, warning systems, shelters, mutual aid, government rescue teams — with some indication of why they help.

assessment_items.question_text: Nayan lives in Gangtok, Sikkim, where winters are very cold and it rains heavily for months. Look at the list of features of mountain life below and explain why each one makes sense for the cold, wet mountain climate. Choose any TWO: (a) wooden houses with slanting roofs (b) thick warm clothes like the bakhu (c) foods like thukpa (a hot noodle soup).
expected_elements: For wooden houses with slanting roofs: an explanation connecting the slanting roof to heavy rain or snow — slanted roofs allow rain or snow to slide off rather than accumulate and damage the structure; wood is locally available in forested mountain regions.

For the bakhu (thick warm clothing): an explanation connecting the thick, layered garment to the cold mountain climate — the cold temperatures require insulating clothing to keep the body warm; thick fabrics trap heat.

For thukpa (hot noodle soup): an explanation connecting a warm, filling soup to the cold climate — hot foods warm the body in cold weather; a nourishing soup is practical when you need to stay warm and energised.
assessment_items.annotation: Students choose any two of the three features. Mark on the quality of the explanation — the reasoning must connect the feature to the climate (cold or wet), not merely describe the feature. Accept responses in any order.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe how climate conditions in a mountain region shape the animals, plants, clothing, food, and shelter of the people who live there.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: For slanting roofs: the reasoning links the roof's slope to heavy rainfall or snowfall — water or snow slides off rather than collecting and causing damage; wood is available in forested mountain regions.
For the bakhu: the reasoning links the thick, warm garment to cold temperatures — insulating material keeps the body warm in a climate where temperatures drop significantly.

For thukpa: the reasoning links a hot soup to cold weather — warmth from hot food is practical and comforting; thukpa is nourishing and suited to physically demanding mountain life in cold conditions.

assessment_items.task: Draw the landform of your own region in the space below. Label your drawing with at least four of these: the name of the area, the type of landform, what people do for work, a food that people eat, what houses look like, a plant or tree that grows there, an animal found there. Then write two sentences explaining how one of your labels connects to the landform itself — why does this place have this feature?
assessment_items.scaffold: Step 1: Draw your local landscape — show the shape of the land (flat, hilly, near water, etc.). Step 2: Add at least four labels from this list: area name / landform type / work people do / a local food / house type / a plant or tree / an animal. Step 3: Write two sentences: 'One feature I labelled is ___ . This connects to my landform because ___.'
format_of_output: A labelled drawing of the student's local landform with at least four labels
Two written sentences explaining how one labelled feature connects to the landform
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any landform that reflects the student's genuine local environment — plains, hills, river valley, coastal, semi-arid, etc. The four labels must be drawn from the list in the task. The two sentences must show reasoning (the 'because') not just description. Regional variation in every label is expected and correct — there is no single right answer for the drawing. Mark on the quality of the connection made in the written sentences.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent a real or imagined environment creatively through drawing and labelling, and reason about how geographical features shape life for the people, animals, and plants within them.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can represent their own geographical and cultural environment through a creative annotated drawing and articulate at least one causal connection between a landform feature and a cultural or natural element of life in that region.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold walks students through three steps. Check: (1) is the drawing a genuine attempt to represent the local landscape shape, not just a decorative picture? (2) are at least four labels from the provided list present? (3) do the two sentences include a 'because' that connects the label to the landform, not just to the student's preference?
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: the drawing shows a recognisable landscape type with specific, accurate labels, and the two sentences name a feature AND explain its connection to the landform with clear reasoning (e.g., 'We have flat fields because the land here is level and the soil is good for farming'). Weak: the drawing is generic with few or no labels, or the two sentences describe a feature without explaining why it relates to the landform.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may use simple shapes and lines to represent the landscape — the labels and sentences carry the cognitive weight. Students who struggle with two full sentences may write the sentence frame with their own words filled in. Any local landform is valid — do not require students to conform to the chapter's four example regions.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Labelled drawing with two written explanatory sentences
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The drawing task matches the C&E dominant mode of the period and the chapter's synthesising activity at p. 149. The written sentences ensure creative expression is paired with geographical reasoning, reflecting the C-4.2 competency's emphasis on observing and describing cultural diversity in the immediate environment.
